wordOrder.title: Put the words in order
wordOrder.subtitle: Tap the words below to build each sentence in the right order. Twenty original sentences, mixing both tenses.

matching.title: Match the signal word to the tense
matching.subtitle: Tap a signal word or phrase, then tap the tense it points to. Finished actions, events and sequences take the past simple; ‘while’, ‘as’ and ‘this time yesterday’ point to an action in progress.

timedMC.title: Beat the clock
timedMC.subtitle: 15 seconds per question. British English. Ask yourself: is it a completed action or an action in progress? That decides the tense.

errorCorrection.title: Find the mistake
errorCorrection.subtitle: Each sentence has exactly one mistake. Tap the word you think is wrong. Twenty original sentences.

items.message: Completed actions in sequence take the past simple.
The reading was the longer action in progress — use the past continuous.
‘While’ introduces the longer action in progress — use the past continuous.
A quick reaction is a short completed action — use the past simple.
‘Want’ is a stative verb — it is not used in the continuous.
After ‘were you’ the verb needs -ing for an action in progress.
‘While’ introduces the longer action in progress — use the past continuous.
With ‘they’ the past continuous needs ‘were’.
Losing something is a completed event at a finished time — use the past simple.
‘At that moment’ shows an action in progress — use the past continuous.
The past continuous negative is ‘wasn’t’ + -ing, with no ‘didn’t’.
After ‘didn’t’ use the base verb.
‘As’ introduces the action in progress — use the past continuous.
Scene-setting next to ‘were singing’ — use the past continuous.
Completed events take the past simple.
‘Know’ is a stative verb — it is not used in the continuous.
A single completed event takes the past simple.
‘In 1975’ is a finished time — use the past simple.
Breaking a leg is a short completed event — use the past simple.
‘This time yesterday’ points to an action in progress — use the past continuous.

levelCheck.title: How well do you know it?
levelCheck.subtitle: 20 mixed questions — typing, word order, signal words, multiple choice, and spot-the-mistake. One pass, then a breakdown of where you’re strong and where to go back and practise.

items.sentText: We {{blank}} a great film last weekend.
items.explain: ‘Last weekend’ is a finished time — use the past simple.

items.sentText: At that moment, the children {{blank}} in the park.
items.explain: ‘At that moment’ — an action in progress: past continuous.

items.sentText: Sam {{blank}} his leg while he was running.
items.explain: A short event during a longer action — use the past simple (‘hurt’ is irregular and does not change).

items.sentText: As I {{blank}} to music, the doorbell rang.
items.explain: ‘As’ introduces the action in progress — use the past continuous.

wrongReasons: ‘While’ introduces a longer action in progress — not a completed one.
‘While’ is about a past action in progress, not a link to now.
‘While’ in a past story points to an action in progress, not a present habit.
items.explain: ‘While’ — an action in progress: past continuous.

wrongReasons: ‘Yesterday’ names a finished time — the past simple for a completed action.
‘Yesterday’ is finished — the present perfect is not used with it.
‘Yesterday’ is a simple finished time — no earlier past is needed.

items.text: Which tense does ‘this time last year’ point to?
wrongReasons: ‘This time last year’ points to a moment in progress — the past simple is for completed actions.
‘This time last year’ is finished — the present perfect does not fit.
‘This time last year’ is in the past, not the present.
items.explain: ‘This time last year’ — an action in progress: past continuous.

wrongReasons: ‘Suddenly’ shows a short event, not an action in progress.
‘Suddenly’ is about a past event, not a link to now.
‘Suddenly’ is a simple past event — no earlier past is needed.
